summary: Describes how SCTP maps into the sockets programming interface. It aims for compatibility with TCP applications while providing access to SCTP features and a unified way to handle events and errors. This is an informational document for programmers.

plainLanguage.summary: Programs talk over the network through a standard door called sockets. This explains how to use that door for SCTP, a protocol like TCP, so programmers can use its extra features.

subtitle: How programs use SCTP through the familiar sockets API, in one-to-one and one-to-many styles.

tldr.problem: SCTP combines TCP-like connections with UDP-like messages and adds features such as multiple streams and multiple addresses, so the existing sockets calls do not map onto it neatly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two socket styles (one-to-many with SOCK_SEQPACKET, one-to-one with SOCK_STREAM), ancillary data for per-message options, event notifications, socket options and new functions such as sctp_bindx() and sctp_peeloff().
tldr.outcome: Most TCP applications can move to SCTP with few changes, and programs can still reach SCTP-specific features. Some older elements are marked deprecated.

today: RFC 6458 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the SCTP sockets API as of December 2011, including which elements were already deprecated at that point.

sections.title: Goals of the SCTP Sockets Mapping
sections.content:
The sockets API gave TCP (RFC 793) and UDP (RFC 768) a standard programming interface across many operating systems. SCTP provides many TCP characteristics but also semantics closer to UDP. This RFC maps it onto sockets so that existing TCP applications can be migrated with few, if any, changes, while still giving access to new SCTP features.

There are three design objectives: stay consistent with existing sockets APIs, support a one-to-many style interface (like a UDP socket that talks to many peers), and support a one-to-one style interface (like a TCP socket). Goals 2 and 3 are not compatible, so the RFC defines both styles. All new SCTP features work with both. The document uses POSIX data types such as uint16_t.

Several elements are marked deprecated. They were introduced, implemented and later replaced, but remain in some implementations. New implementations must implement at least the non-deprecated elements, and those wanting interoperability with older API versions should include the deprecated ones too.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP is like a phone call that can also carry separate little notes. The doorway lets old programs use it like a normal call, or lets new ones use the extra notes.

sections.title: The Two Socket Styles
sections.content:
In the one-to-many style, one socket represents many associations. The socket is created with SOCK_SEQPACKET, and each association gets an identifier of type sctp_assoc_t. A server uses socket(), bind(), listen(), recvmsg(), sendmsg() and close(). It does not call accept(), which should return EOPNOTSUPP; new associations arrive automatically and are announced by an SCTP_ASSOC_CHANGE event. Clients skip listen().

In the one-to-one style, the socket is created with SOCK_STREAM and controls one association, connected at most once, as with TCP. A server uses socket(), bind(), listen() and accept(), which returns a new descriptor for each association. A client uses socket() and connect().

With either style the domain is PF_INET (IPv4 only) or PF_INET6 (IPv6 and IPv4), and the protocol is IPPROTO_SCTP. An association can be branched off a one-to-many socket into a one-to-one socket with sctp_peeloff(), useful for moving high-volume associations to their own descriptors.
sections.plainLanguage: One style is a switchboard that handles many callers on one line. The other is a normal phone line for one caller. You can move a busy caller from the switchboard to their own line.

sections.title: Binding, Connecting and Closing
sections.content:
An endpoint can have several addresses but only one local port. bind() can be called only once. To bind several addresses, or to add or delete addresses when the extension in RFC 5061 is supported, use sctp_bindx(). If an application does not call bind() first, the system picks an ephemeral port and an address set like a wildcard bind, which automatically enables SCTP multi-homing. Until listen() is called, the endpoint rejects an inbound INIT with an ABORT.

Associations can be set up implicitly: calling sendmsg() or sendto() toward a peer with no association makes the stack create one, with an SCTP_COMM_UP notification on both sides. SCTP allows data during setup, so an application wanting this uses sendto() or sendmsg() rather than connect(). SCTP has no half close, so MSG_EOF must not be used when initiating a connection.

On a one-to-many socket, close() gracefully shuts down all associations, while one association is ended by sendmsg() with SCTP_EOF (graceful) or SCTP_ABORT. For one-to-one sockets, shutdown() with SHUT_WR starts an immediate full SCTP shutdown, unlike TCP's half close, so ported code that uses shutdown() may need to change.

One caution: on a one-to-many socket sharing a single buffer, one stalled association can block sending on all of them. The RFC suggests per-association buffer space, non-blocking sockets, or one-to-one sockets.
sections.plainLanguage: You pick which doors and which phone numbers to use. Hanging up gently lets everyone finish talking, and hanging up fast just cuts the line. One stuck caller should not block everyone else.

sections.title: Ancillary Data and Notifications
sections.content:
Per-message SCTP options travel as ancillary data in the msg_control field of sendmsg() and recvmsg(), with cmsg_level set to IPPROTO_SCTP. Structures include SCTP_INIT (association setup parameters), SCTP_SNDINFO and SCTP_RCVINFO, plus SCTP_PRINFO and SCTP_AUTHINFO. The older SCTP_SNDRCV and SCTP_EXTRCV are deprecated.

In SCTP_SNDINFO, snd_sid picks the stream, snd_ppid is passed to the peer unchanged, and snd_context comes back if the send fails. Flags include SCTP_UNORDERED, SCTP_ADDR_OVER, SCTP_ABORT, SCTP_EOF and SCTP_SENDALL.

Events arrive through recvmsg() as notifications, such as SCTP_ASSOC_CHANGE, SCTP_PEER_ADDR_CHANGE, SCTP_SHUTDOWN_EVENT and SCTP_SEND_FAILED_EVENT. The association-change states are SCTP_COMM_UP, SCTP_COMM_LOST, SCTP_RESTART, SCTP_SHUTDOWN_COMP and SCTP_CANT_STR_ASSOC. Applications choose notifications with the SCTP_EVENT option. If SCTP_ASSOC_CHANGE is disabled, the application must correlate messages to associations using the peer address in msg_name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message can carry a little sticky note saying which lane to use or how to treat it. The system also sends news flashes, like a call connecting or dropping.

sections.title: Socket Options and New Functions
sections.content:
Section 8 groups socket options into read/write, read-only and write-only. Examples include SCTP_RTOINFO (retransmission timeouts), SCTP_INITMSG (initialization parameters, such as stream counts), SCTP_NODELAY, SCTP_AUTOCLOSE, SCTP_PRIMARY_ADDR, SCTP_PEER_ADDR_PARAMS, SCTP_DELAYED_SACK, SCTP_FRAGMENT_INTERLEAVE and the authentication options built on RFC 4895. SCTP_STATUS reports association status.

Section 9 adds functions the standard calls cannot express: sctp_bindx(), sctp_peeloff(), sctp_getpaddrs() and sctp_getladdrs() with their free counterparts, sctp_connectx(), and the newer sctp_sendv() and sctp_recvv(). Older sctp_sendmsg(), sctp_recvmsg(), sctp_send() and sctp_sendx() are deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a control panel of dials for tuning how SCTP behaves, and a few extra tools for jobs the old doorway never had to do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If the platform has privileged users, the SCTP implementation should restrict bind() and sctp_bindx() on port numbers below 1024 to them, as many TCP and UDP implementations do. Unprivileged users should not be able to set parameters, such as struct sctp_rtoinfo, that make congestion control more aggressive than allowed on the public Internet.

Applications using one-to-many sockets with interleave level 0 are subject to denial-of-service attacks, described under SCTP_FRAGMENT_INTERLEAVE. For transport layer security, applications can use DTLS/SCTP (RFC 6083) through this API.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted users should get the special low-numbered doors, and nobody should be allowed to turn up the speed so high it jams the network.
